terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; impersonal accidit, with the dative of the person and ut with the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Fam. 14.8.1: sī quid acciderit novī
Caes. BG 4.29.1: accidit ut esset lūna plēna
terms.comment: Of what happens unexpectedly, and above all of what goes wrong: sī quid adversī acciderit (Cic. Ac. 2.121, Lewis & Short). What happens is the subject, or an ut-clause; the person it happens to goes in the dative: quid tibi accidit?.

terms.grammar: verb, irregular: the passive of faciō
terms.comment: The everyday word: quid fit?, what’s going on?; ut fit, as usually happens; fit ut, it comes about that (see what happened?).

evidence: Sen. Ep. 24.13: hoc nōbīs quoque majusculīs puerīs ēvenit
Ter. Ph. 65–66: ēvēnit senibus ambōbus simul iter … ut esset
terms.comment: Of things good or bad, especially as they turn out in the end.

terms.gloss: happen (to someone), usually of good luck
evidence: Gell. 9.3.5: quod nāscī contigit temporibus vītae tuae
Quint. 1.1.7: quibus discere ipsīs nōn contigit
terms.comment: With the dative and an infinitive or ut: what someone has the luck to do.

terms.gloss: come up, fall to one’s lot

phrases.latin: Item posthāc, sī quid opus erit, sī quid acciderit novī, faciēs ut sciam.
phrases.english: And in future too, if anything is needed, if anything new happens, let me know.

phrases.latin: Eādem nocte accidit ut esset lūna plēna
phrases.english: That same night it happened that there was a full moon

phrases.latin: sed heus tū! quid agis? ecquid fit?
phrases.english: but hey, you! How are you? Anything happening?

phrases.latin: fēcit statim, ut fit, fastīdium cōpia
phrases.english: plenty, as usually happens, soon bred boredom

accidi.against: Lewis & Short ac-cĭdo, cīdi, the perfect of ac-cīdo, cut down
accidi.html: A compound of cadō, cecidī; Lewis & Short marks the perfect short in the other compounds: dē-cĭdo, cĭdi; incĭdo, cĭdi; occĭdo, cĭdi.
